To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of sodium transport across a sodium-transporting cell is determined not by the sodium concentration in the cytoplasm but by the sodium conductance (or permeability) of the apical membrane and that the conductance of the basolateral barrier to potassium is determined not by its potassium conductance but by the rate of sodium-potassium exchange across it.

the intracellular sodium activity is inversely related to the sodium conductance (Pn) of the apical membrane and that the rate of sodium efflux (Jn) is directly related to the conductance of the basolateral barrier to potassium (Pm) in several epithelia.

the rate of sodium absorption by the frog skin is regulated, in part, by a "flush-through" mechanism that is based upon an inverse relation between the intracellular sodium activity (as reflected by the mucosal-to-serosal sodium diffusion potential) and the sodium conductances of both the apical and basolateral membranes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of sodium-transporting cells.

the mechanisms of regulation of transepithelial transport of water and electrolytes in mammalian renal and intestinal epithelia, particularly in relation to the control of sodium and water reabsorption.

the regulation of the transcellular sodium flux in sodium-transport epithelia, and the present review focuses on two mechanisms which appear to protect the cell from marked changes in its sodium content.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the epithelial sodium transport cell is endowed with two intrinsic regulatory mechanisms that are activated in response to changes in the rate of sodium transport.
the homocellular mechanisms are "flush-through" regulatory mechanisms.
the homocellular mechanisms are "sodium-activated sodium conductances" and "pump-leak coupling."
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

these two mechanisms, which appear to operate independently of one another, are capable of maintaining the sodium and potassium content of the absorptive cell in a relatively narrow range in the face of marked changes in sodium transport.
the epithelium "flushes itself through" by increasing the rate of transepithelial fluid absorption when sodium transport is increased.

these mechanisms, which are not present in the red blood cell, appear to serve the purpose of maintaining intracellular sodium activity at a relatively constant level, and of preventing the intracellular potassium content from falling too low.
The main takeaway from our work is that
epithelia with high sodium transport rates are protected by the operation of these mechanisms from extinction by "flush through".

epithelial sodium transport systems are not "extinction prone" in the sense that they do not "run out of fuel" or "burn out" in the face of rapid and wide-ranging changes in the rate of sodium transport.
these mechanisms are not "hard-wired" and can be modified in response to chronic changes in sodium transport rate.
